answers.text:
"Superposition" is the term Anthropic's interpretability team uses for a specific way a neural network can pack information: when a layer has, say, four neurons, but the underlying data has many more independent features than that, the network can still represent all of them by letting individual neurons respond to combinations of several unrelated features rather than one feature each. The article's own worked example is the "highly-distributed" code: there's another kind of distributed representation that can represent all colored shapes with only 4 neurons (just as 4 bits can represent 16 numbers), and it's maximal superposition in the piece's terminology. The catch, spelled out just after, is that it isn't possible to generically select most colors or shapes with a linear probe, let alone sets — you gain capacity but lose the ability to read a feature back out with a simple linear readout; you need a nonlinearity to disentangle the overlapping signals.

This isn't a term the article coins from scratch; as you may know, it comes from an earlier Anthropic paper this note is building on, "Toy Models of Superposition" (Elhage et al., 2022), which showed that small ReLU networks trained on sparse synthetic features will represent more features than they have dimensions by overlapping them in this way, at the cost of interference that a nonlinearity has to filter out. The present article's whole argument is that this "superposition" strategy is one of two things people conflate under the umbrella term "distributed representations" — the other being "composition," the more familiar idea of independent features (like Mikolov's word-embedding directions for "gender" or "plural") combining additively. The selected word sits right in the piece's title and thesis: the two ideas are being pulled apart because, as the note argues, if one has \(m\) bits to encode stimuli, we can think of there as being \(\exp(m)\) volume... if there's no composition, one can instead store \(\exp(m)\) items in superposition, although a non-linearity is required to retrieve them.

answers.asked: An informal note on the relationship between superposition and distributed representations by Chris Olah.
answers.text:
Chris Olah is a machine learning researcher known for co-founding and leading interpretability work at Anthropic, and before that for his research at OpenAI and Google Brain on visualizing and understanding neural network internals (he's also known for the widely-read "colah's blog" on deep learning). He's one of the principal figures behind Anthropic's "Transformer Circuits Thread" — the research venue this piece belongs to, as flagged by the very first line of the article — which focuses on mechanistic interpretability: trying to reverse-engineer what's actually happening inside neural networks rather than treating them as black boxes.

The phrase "informal note" is doing real work here, and the article itself explains what that means a bit further down: informal notes allow the team to publish ideas that aren't as refined and developed as a full paper, and mistakes are possible. The reader is asked to treat it more like ideas a colleague is informally sharing, or a typical internet blog post, rather than a paper. So the framing signals that what follows is exploratory thinking rather than a polished, peer-reviewed result — closer to a research memo than a finished paper.

"Superposition" refers to a specific phenomenon Olah and colleagues had studied in earlier work (referenced later in the piece as "Toy Models of Superposition"): the idea that a neural network can represent more features than it has neurons by overlapping them in the same set of neurons, at the cost of needing nonlinear computation to untangle them again. "Distributed representations" is an older, broader term from neuroscience and connectionist AI for the general idea that concepts are encoded across many neurons at once rather than one neuron per concept. The note's stated purpose, given just after this selection, is to clarify how superposition relates to this classic idea of distributed representations, after having had time to reflect on the relationship since publishing the original superposition paper.

answers.asked: What does "superposition" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Superposition" here names one of two things people mean by "distributed representations" — the strategy of packing more features into a representation than it has neurons, by letting them overlap, rather than giving each feature its own dedicated neuron or clean combination of neurons [spya-fyxmks]. The article introduces it concretely through Thorpe's "dense" or "highly-distributed" code for shapes and colors, where there's another kind of distributed representation that can represent all colored shapes with only 4 neurons (just as 4 bits can represent 16 numbers), which the author explicitly frames as maximal superposition [spya-c2eewa]. The cost of this compression is that Dense codes like this have a very cool advantage: they can represent far more, totally unrelated objects than there are neurons. But note that there are also lots of costs to this. — in particular, you lose the ability to cleanly read features out with a linear probe, and you lose the ability to represent things "between" features [spya-xwq6ty].

Why it matters to the argument: the piece's central claim is that superposition and composition (features combining, like "green" + "square") are not just two points on a spectrum of "how distributed" a representation is, but two different, competing ways of using the same underlying capacity. It makes this precise with a volume argument: If one has \(m\) bits to encode stimuli, we can think of there as being \(\exp(m)\) volume. Storing \(n\) features which arbitrarily compose together requires \(\exp(n)\) volume; so we can only store fully composable features in \(m\) bits. But if there's no composition, one can instead store \(\exp(m)\) items in superposition, although a non-linearity is required to retrieve them. That is, composition and superposition are two different ways to allocate the exponential volume, which is why the author says maximal superposition and full composition are mutually exclusive — a fully compositional code cannot also be in maximal superposition [spya-kq5p9m spya-jzkekc].

This matters beyond the toy examples because the two strategies have opposite implications for interpretability: composition lets you understand a network in terms of a small, linear set of independent features, while superposition hides features from linear methods and requires nonlinear decoding [spya-armg2f spya-xwq6ty]. The author states this is the whole point of distinguishing them: Understanding the structure of representations is important because they're fundamentally at the heart of efforts to reverse engineer and mechanistically understand neural networks. When neural network representations are distributed in the sense we call "composition", it is possible to understand them in terms of a linear number of independent features rather than an exponential amount of volume. The opening of the piece frames this as the motivation for the whole note: distinguishing composition from superposition is necessary to escape the curse of dimensionality and actually understand what a network's representations are doing [spya-nwuh77].

"Monosemantic" here means having exactly one meaning per unit — a single neuron corresponds to a single, specific thing rather than firing in response to multiple unrelated concepts. In this passage, the "local code" has a separate neuron for each (shape, color) pair, and the article calls this model "monosemantic" and notes it "doesn't have any superposition." Each neuron does exactly one job: there's a neuron that means "red circle," another that means "blue square," and so on, with no overlap.

The term is coined in deliberate contrast to "polysemantic," which shows up later in the piece to describe neurons in the superposition-heavy codes — units that respond to several unrelated features at once (the article uses it in [39] to describe neurons that are "polysemantic, but only respond to a few features"). This monosemantic/polysemantic distinction is the anchor for the whole essay's argument: monosemantic neurons are easy to interpret because each one has a single, clean meaning, but as you'll see in the later "dense" and "semi-distributed" codes, packing more information into fewer neurons than there are features forces individual neurons to become polysemantic, which is exactly the phenomenon the authors call superposition. So this one word is doing double duty — describing the "local code" example concretely, and setting up the interpretability stakes (monosemantic = easy to understand; polysemantic = hard) that motivate why the composition/superposition distinction matters in the first place.

answers.asked: In our language, this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition.
answers.text:
"Monosemantic" here means a neuron that stands for exactly one thing — in this case, one specific (shape, color) pair, like "red circle" or "blue square." Each neuron has a single, fixed meaning; it never gets reused to also mean something else. This is the opposite of "polysemantic," a term the article uses later when discussing neurons that respond to several unrelated features at once.

"Doesn't have any superposition" is the companion claim, and it's making a specific technical point that this article's whole framework depends on. Superposition, in the vocabulary Chris Olah and collaborators developed in their earlier "Toy Models of Superposition" work, is what happens when a network has more features it wants to represent than it has neurons to represent them with — so it's forced to overlap features on top of the same neurons or directions, recoverable only nonlinearly. Here, since there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair, there's no such crowding: every possible thing the code can represent gets its own dedicated neuron, so nothing is sharing space with anything else.

The line is doing setup work for the rest of the piece. Olah is establishing the "local code" as one clean end of the space of possibilities — one neuron, one meaning, zero superposition — precisely so that the following sections (semi-local/compositional codes, then dense/superposed codes) can be shown as pulling apart along two genuinely different axes, composition and superposition, rather than sitting on a single "local to distributed" spectrum as Thorpe's original framing suggested.

answers.asked: What does "monosemantic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
The article uses "monosemantic" in the local code section: describing the pure local code where there's a separate neuron for each (shape, color) pair, it says this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition [spya-kcjqdw]. So here "monosemantic" means a neuron that stands for exactly one thing — one (shape, color) combination — rather than being reused to mean different things in different contexts.

My inference is that this matters to the argument because the local code is the baseline case with no superposition: each neuron has one clean meaning, which is why a linear probe can cleanly find features like "red" in it, though the piece is careful to note that even in that clean case it "doesn't seem like the above example should be understood as having a 'red' feature" [spya-n30s4d], since the neurons are coding for (color, shape) pairs, not for color alone.

The contrast the piece is building toward is with "polysemantic" neurons that come later — in the semi-distributed code, units "begin to have some meaning – they're polysemantic, but only respond to a few features" [spya-vw7xv6], because they're in superposition, standing for more than one thing depending on context. So "monosemantic" versus its opposite is the piece's way of marking whether a neuron carries a single, cleanly separable meaning (no superposition) or several overlapping meanings at once (superposition) — which is exactly the composition/superposition distinction the whole note is built around [spya-fyxmks].
